lesson.title: The Point That Changes Everything: Influential Points
lesson.summary: An influential point is a single observation whose removal noticeably changes the regression line's slope, intercept, or correlation, often because it sits far out on the x-axis.
lesson.body:
Least-squares regression lines are calculated from every point in a data set, but they are not calculated equally from every point. Some observations barely nudge the line if you removed them; others, if deleted, would swing the slope, shift the intercept, or reshape the correlation dramatically. A point in the second category is called an influential point: removing it changes the regression line by an amount large enough to matter for the conclusions you would draw, not merely by an amount large enough to show up in the decimal places.

Return to the study-hours data one final time: (1,55), (2,65), (3,70), (4,80), (5,88), which fits the line y-hat = 47.3 + 8.1x, a strong positive relationship (more hours, higher scores). Now suppose a sixth student is added to the data set: one who reported studying 20 hours but scored only 40 on the exam, perhaps due to illness or an unusual circumstance. Refitting the regression line to all six points, using the computational formulas slope = [sum(xy) - n(x-bar)(y-bar)] / [sum(x-squared) - n(x-bar)-squared], gives a new slope of about -1.46 instead of the original +8.1. Adding just one point flipped the direction of the entire relationship, from strongly positive to negative.

That reversal is the signature of an influential point. The new student's data pulled the whole line toward it because its x-value, 20, is so far from the other x-values (1 through 5) that the line has almost no choice but to swing toward accommodating it. Notice that this single addition did not just shrink r-squared a little; it changed the practical conclusion a reader would draw from the graph, from "studying more predicts higher scores" to "studying more predicts lower scores," which is a dramatic and misleading distortion caused by one data point out of six. A sample size of six is small enough that a single case can dominate the fit this way; the same absolute pull would matter far less in a data set of six hundred points, which is part of why influential points are a particular concern in small classroom-sized data sets.

Influential points are usually points with unusual x-values, extreme in a direction away from the bulk of the data, though a point can also become influential through some combination of an unusual x-value and a residual that runs against the overall pattern. The only reliable way to identify an influential point is to actually compute the regression twice, once with the point and once without it, and compare the resulting slopes, intercepts, or correlation coefficients; if they differ substantially, the point is influential. Some statistical software automates this comparison, but understanding what the software is doing, refitting the line with and without a suspicious case, is what actually builds the intuition.

Because influential points can single-handedly reverse a trend, every regression analysis should include a check for them before conclusions are trusted. It is tempting to simply delete an influential point once it is found, but that decision needs justification beyond "it changes my answer"; a legitimate data entry error is grounds for removal, while a genuine, if unusual, observation may need to be reported and discussed rather than discarded. The next two ideas, leverage and outliers in regression, break the concept of "influence" apart into its two separate ingredients: how extreme a point's x-value is, and how far its y-value strays from the pattern, both of which combine to determine whether a given point actually swings the line.
